[TENTATIVE]
ORDER DENYING SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE
COMPLAINT PURSUANT TO CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE § 425.16


 



I.         BACKGROUND



Defendants allegedly operated
an unlawful and undisclosed capping, referral, kickback and/or fee-splitting
scheme by soliciting patients to Defendant Doctors, who then would provide an
unlawful split to Referring Defendants. Plaintiff-Relator State Farm Mutual
Automobile Insurance Company (“State Farm”) sues Defendants on behalf of the
People of the State of California for violation of the insurance frauds
prevention act.



On March 24, 2026,
Defendants Kenneth Light, M.D., and Kenneth I. Light, M.D., Inc. (collectively “Light”)
filed the instant special motion to strike (or “anti-SLAPP motion”) under Code
of Civil Procedure section 425.16.[1]
State Farm opposed. Light replied.



The Court held an
initial hearing on this motion on June 5, 2026.  At the hearing,
the Court asked several questions and counsel for the moving parties and State
Farm responded. State Farm clarified that it was not attacking the use of liens on
potential money judgments to pay for medical treatment. Instead, State
Farm alleges that Defendant Doctors employed Referring Defendants as runners or
cappers in violation of Insurance Code section 1871.7.  Counsel for the moving
parties Ghomri and Light clarified that Ghomri and Light
treated their patients the same, regardless of whether they
were referred by the Referring Defendants or
otherwise. Ghomri and Light used the same process and generated the
same type of reports for all patients. The Court continued the matter to
today’s hearing date.  



 



II.        OBJECTIONS



The Court rules on State
Farm’s objections as follows:



The
Court sustains State Farm’s fifth and seventh objections.



The
Court overrules State Farm’s other objections.



The Court rules on Light’s
objections as follows:



The Court sustains Light’s second
and third objections.



The Court overrules Light’s
other objections.



 



III.      LEGAL STANDARD



“Litigation
of an anti-SLAPP motion involves a two-step process. First, ‘the moving
defendant bears the burden of establishing that the challenged allegations or
claims ‘aris[e] from’ protected activity in which the defendant has engaged.’
[Citation.] Second, for each claim that does arise from protected activity, the
plaintiff must show the claim has “at least ‘minimal merit.’ [Citation.]”  (Bonni v. St. Joseph Health System
(2021) 11 Cal.5th 995, 1009, citations omitted.)  To separate communications which form the
source of the dispute from those that merely provide evidence of it, courts ask
whether “the same dispute would exist” if there were no pending threat of
litigation.  (Gotterba v. Travolta
(2014) 228 Cal.App.4th 35, 42.)



As
to the second step of the inquiry, a plaintiff seeking to demonstrate the merit
of the claim “may not rely solely on its complaint, even if verified; instead,
its proof must be made upon competent admissible evidence.”  (Sweetwater
Union High School District v. Gilbane Building Co. (2019) 6 Cal.5th 931,
940, citations omitted.)



A
party opposing a special motion to strike has the burden to “state [] and
substantiate [] a legally sufficient claim.” 
(Navellier v. Sletten (2002) 29 Cal.4th 82, 88 & 93.)  “‘Put another way, the party “must
demonstrate that the complaint is both legally sufficient and supported by a
sufficient prima facie showing of facts to sustain a favorable judgment if the
evidence submitted by the defendant is credited.”’ [Citations.]”  (Id. at pgs. 88-89.)  To that end, the party must present competent
evidence, “that would be admissible at trial.” 
(HMS Capital, Inc. v. Lawyers Title Co. (2004) 118 Cal.App.4th
204, 212.)  “[D]eclarations may not be
based upon ‘information and belief’ [citation]” and documents submitted without
the proper foundation will not be considered. 
(Id.)  The complaint, even
if verified, is insufficient to carry the plaintiff’s shifted burden.  (Roberts v. Los Angeles County Bar
Association (2003) 105 Cal.App.4th 604, 614; Karnazes v. Ares (2016)
244 Cal.App.4th 344, 354 [“pleadings do not constitute evidence”]; see also
Burke, Anti-SLAPP Litigation (The Rutter Group, Civil Litigation Series 2018
§5:13) [“To satisfy prong two, the plaintiff must submit admissible evidence
that if credited is sufficient to sustain a favorable judgment against the legal
theories asserted by the defendant.”].)



“A
cause of action is subject to a special motion to strike if the defendant shows
that the cause of action arises from an act in furtherance of the defendant’s
constitutional right of petition or free speech in connection with a public
issue and the plaintiff fails to demonstrate a probability of prevailing on the
claim. [Citations.]”  (Digerati
Holdings, LLC v. Young Money Entertainment, LLC (2011) 194 Cal.App.4th 873,
883.) 



“An
‘act in furtherance of a person’s right of petition or free speech under the
United States or California Constitution in connection with a public issue’ is
defined by statute to include ‘(1) any written or oral statement or writing
made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other
official proceeding authorized by law, (2) any written or oral statement or
writing made in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a
legislative, executive, or judicial body, or any other official proceeding
authorized by law, (3) any written or oral statement or writing made in a place
open to the public or a public forum in connection with an issue of public
interest, or (4) any other conduct in furtherance of the exercise of the constitutional
right of petition or the constitutional right of free speech in connection with
a public issue or an issue of public interest.’ 
[Citation.] If the defendant shows that the cause of action arises from a
statement described in clause (1) or (2) of section 425.16, subdivision (e),
the defendant is not required to separately demonstrate that the statement was
made in connection with a ‘public issue.’ [Citation.]”  (Id.)



“A cause of action is one ‘arising from’ protected activity
within the meaning of section 425.16, subdivision (b)(1) only if the
defendant’s act on which the cause of action is based was an act in furtherance
of the defendant’s constitutional right of petition or free speech in
connection with a public issue. [Citation.] In deciding whether the ‘arising
from’ requirement is satisfied, ‘the court shall consider the pleadings, and
supporting and opposing affidavits stating the facts upon which the liability or
defense is based.’ [(Code Civ. Proc.. § 425.16(b)(2).)] Whether the ‘arising
from’ requirement is satisfied depends on the ‘gravamen or principal thrust’ of
the claim. [(Episcopal Church Cases (2009) 45 Cal.4th 467, 477, quoting Martinez
v. Metabolife International, Inc. (2003) 113 Cal.App.4th 181, 193.)] A
cause of action does not arise from protected activity for purposes of the
anti-SLAPP statute if the protected activity is merely incidental to the cause
of action. [(Martinez, 113 Cal.App.4th at pg. 188.)]”  (Digerati Holdings, LLC, 194
Cal.App.4th at pgs. 883-884.)  To show
that a claim arises from protected activity under §425.16(b)(1), it is not
sufficient to show that the claim “was filed after, or because of, protected
activity, or when protected activity merely provides evidentiary support or
context for the claim.”  (Rand
Resources, LLC v. City of Carson (2019) 6 Cal.5th 610, 621.)  “Rather, the protected activity must ‘supply
elements of the challenged claim.’ [Citation.]” 
(Id., citations omitted.)



“At
the first step, the moving defendant bears the burden of identifying all
allegations of protected activity, and the claims for relief supported by them.
When relief is sought based on allegations of both protected and unprotected
activity, the unprotected activity is disregarded at this stage.”  (Baral v. Schnitt (2016) 1 Cal.5th
376, 396, emphasis added.)  



 



IV.       DISCUSSION



Light requests the Court strike the complaint
as the cause of action asserted against Light arises from Light’s protected exercise
of free speech or petition rights. Pursuant to section 425.16, subdivision (b),
a cause of action against a person arising from the person’s right of petition
or free speech shall be subject to a special motion to strike unless the court
determines the plaintiff has established there is a probability the plaintiff
will prevail on the claim.



A.        Anti-SLAPP Analysis



1.         Protected Activity



Light asserts Light’s
activity is protected, satisfying the first prong of an anti-SLAPP motion, as
it consists of Light’s medical report and invoices being communicated by legal
counsel to State Farm as part of personal injury lawsuits brought by Light’s
patients against State Farm’s insured clients, or as part of settlement demands
made in anticipation of litigation. (Mot., Light Decl. ¶¶ 3-7.) The Anti-SLAPP
statute defines relevant protected activity as follows:



“(1)
any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive,
or judicial proceeding, or any other official proceeding authorized by law, (2)
any written or oral statement or writing made in connection with an issue under
consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or judicial body, or any
other official proceeding authorized by law, (3) any written or oral statement
or writing made in a place open to the public or a public forum in connection
with an issue of public interest, or (4) any other conduct in furtherance of
the exercise of the constitutional right of petition or the constitutional
right of free speech in connection with a public issue or an issue of public
interest.” (§ 425.16, subd. (e).)



Courts have “have adopted a
fairly expansive view of what constitutes litigation-related activities within
the scope of section 425.16.” (Kashian v. Harriman (2002) 98 Cal.App.4th
892, 908.) “Correspondence made in anticipation of litigation “contemplated in
good faith and under serious consideration can be a petitioning activity
protected by the anti-SLAPP statute.” (Lunada Biomedical v. Nunez (2014)
230 Cal.App.4th 459, 472.) The burden is on the moving party to make this
initial showing. (Navellier v. Sletten (2002) 29 Cal.4th 82, 88.)



People ex. rel. Allstate
Ins. Co. v. Rubin (2021)
66 Cal.App.5th 493 is instructive here. In Rubin, an insurance company
brought suit against a physician and related medical providers, alleging the
physician prepare fraudulent patient medical reports and billing statement in
support of insurance claims. (Ibid.) The physician brought an anti-SLAPP
motion on the basis the lawsuit arose from the protected activity of preparing
and submitted medical records in anticipation of litigation. (Id. at
496.) The trial court denied the motion, which the appellate court affirmed, as
prelitigation communication may only constitute protected activity if it is
related to litigation contemplated in good faith and under serious
consideration. (Id. at 496, 499.) If litigation is only a possibility,
it is not under serious consideration. (Id. at 499.) “Thus, for
example, when a cause of action arises from conduct that is a ‘necessary
prerequisite’ to litigation, but will lead to litigation only if negotiations
fail or contractual commitments are not honored, future litigation is merely
theoretical rather than anticipated and the conduct is therefore not protected
prelitigation activity.” (Ibid., citing Bel Air Internet, LLC v.
Morales (2018) 20 Cal.App.5th 924, 941.)



“The submission of claims
to an insurer for payment in the regular course of business prior to the
commencement of litigation is not an act ‘in furtherance of [the] right[ ] of
petition’ within the meaning of the anti-SLAPP statute.” (Id. at 499.) Protecting
reports and claims under section 425.16 because they eventually could be used
in connection with an official proceeding would effectively provide immunity
for any type of criminal fraud, so long as the defrauding party is willing to
go to court. (Ibid., citing People ex rel. 20th Century Ins. Co. v.
Building Permit Consultants, Inc. (2000) 86 Cal.App.4th 280, 285.) Furthermore,
the filing of allegedly false insurance claims is also not protected under the
anti-SLAPP statute. (Id. at 499, citing to People ex rel. Fire Ins.
Exchange v. Anapol (2012) 211 Cal.App.4th 809.)



The court specifically held
that, because the documents were prepared to be utilized, and render payment to
the physician, for any settlement, judgment, or verdict, there remains a
possibility of resolving claims outside of court. (Id. at 500-501.)
Therefore, the documents were not made in good faith and in serious
consideration of litigation. (Id. at 502.) The activity was not
protected under section 425.16.



Here, Light has
specifically stated Light’s medical reports and invoices were communicated by
legal counsel “as part of settlement demands in anticipation of litigation that
is contemplated in good faith.” (Light Decl. ¶ 3.) However, Light’s declaration does
not indicate his medical reports and invoices are any
different or otherwise specially prepared if they were going to
be used to bring personal injury claims against State Farm’s insured.  Counsel
for Light candidly agreed Light treated all
of his patients the same way.  Light’s reports and
invoices were prepared by the same process, regardless of
whether the patient was allegedly referred by the Referring
Defendants or not.  Just as in Rubin, the preparation
of medical reports and bills in support of insurance claims are Light’s routine
and usual course of business. (See Anapol, supra, 211
Cal.App.4th at p. 827 [“ ‘[t]he submission of contractual claims for
payment in the regular course of business’ is not an act in
furtherance of the right of petition”].) In addition, Light’s medical
reports may or may not end up
being used  in litigation. Unless negotiations with
State Farm failed or State Farm denied a demand for
payment, litigation is simply a possibility. (Rubin, supra, at p. 502
[“That is, unless negotiations with Allstate failed, or Allstate denied a
demand for payment, litigation was simply a possibility, and
that ‘possibility’ of litigation does not rise to protected
prelitigation activity under the anti-SLAPP statute.”]; see Mission
Beverage Co. v. Pabst Brewing Co., LLC, supra, 15 Cal.App.5th at pp. 702,
703 [litigation is not “ ‘under [serious] consideration’ ” if it is
only a “ ‘possibility’ ”].) 



Light has not satisfied the
initial burden of demonstrating Light’s activity is protected under section
425.16. Therefore, the Court denies the instant motion.



2.         Public
Interest Exception



In State Farm’s opposition,
State Farm argues the anti-SLAPP statute does apply to the subject action, as
this action was brought “solely in the public interest or on behalf of the
general public,” as this is a qui tam Insurance Fraud Prevention Act
(“IFPA”) suit brought on behalf of the State of California. (§ 425.17, subd.
(b).) The public interest exception applies to actions brought on behalf of the
general public so long as (1) the plaintiff does not seek relief greater than
or different from the relief sought for the general public or a class of which
the plaintiff is a member; (2) the action, if successful, would enforce an
important right affecting the public interest, and would confer a significant
benefit to the general public or large class of persons; and (3) private
enforcement is necessary and places a disproportionate financial burden on the
plaintiff in relation to the plaintiff’s stake in the matter. (Ibid.)



State Farm argues qui
tam IFPA actions satisfy these requirements. “Qui tam action[s] brought by
[a] relator ‘on behalf of the general public’ under Insurance Code Section
1871.7 falls within the public interest exception of section 425.17(b).” (People
ex rel. Strathmann v. Acacia Research Corp. (2012) 210
Cal. App. 4th 487, 492.)  State Farm
asserts this claim is limited to only relief available under Insurance Code
section 1871.7, (i.e. “the bounty available under Insurance Code section
1871.7, subdivision (g)(2)(A).”) complying with the relief requirements. (See Strathmann,
supra, 210 Cal.4th at pg. 503.) This action, if successful, would
enforce an important right in protecting the public from higher premiums
stemming from fraudulent insurance claims. (Id. at 504.) Finally,
private enforcement of this action is necessary because there is no evidence of
a public official intending to prosecute the action, as no such official has
intervened to prosecute. (Ibid.) The fact no public entity has sought to
enforce these rights is sufficient to establish private enforcement is
necessary. (The Inland Oversight Comm. v. Cty. San Bernardino (2015) 239
Cal. App. 4th 671, 676.)



The Court acknowledges State Farm’s argument but does not
rule on the issue presented as the Court has otherwise already found grounds to
deny the instant motion.



B.        Fees
and Costs



State Farm requests the
Court award costs and reasonable attorney’s fees, as the motion to strike is frivolous.
Under section 425.16, subdivision (c)(1), a prevailing plaintiff is entitled to
costs and reasonable attorney’s fees if the court finds an anti-SLAPP motion is
frivolous or solely intended to cause unnecessary delay.



“A motion is totally and
completely without merit for purposes of a finding of frivolousness under
section 425.16, subdivision (c)(1) or section 128.5 only if any reasonable
attorney would agree that the motion is totally devoid of merit. [Citation.]
This is an objective standard. Whether the sole purpose of the motion is to
harass an opposing party or the motion is solely intended to cause unnecessary
delay, in contrast, concerns the subjective motivation of the moving defendant.
[Citation.] The moving defendant's subjective motivation can be inferred from
the absence of any arguable merit. [Citation.]” (Chitsazzadeh v. Kramer
& Kaslow (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 676, 683–84.)



State Farm argues the
motion was completely without merit, as Light inexplicably failed
to address Rubin when filing this
motion.  Instead Light relied upon vague definitions
without direct applicability and omitted context and
distinctions.  Rubin is on point.  In
addition, Rubin addressed attorney’s fees and concluded
Rubin’s similar arguments were meritless but not frivolous.  Here,
however, we have the benefit of Rubin.  A reasonable
attorney would have been aware of Rubin and
other unambiguous case law holding allegedly fraudulent physician
documentation, prepared in anticipation of potential settlement, is not protected
activity under section 425.16.  (Baharian-Mehr v. Smith (2010)
189 Cal. App. 4th 265, 275.)  Therefore, the Court finds the motion
frivolous under section 425.16, subdivision (c)(1) and
so grants attorney’s fees and costs.  



State Farm requests fees in $7,800.00, based upon 15 hours
of attorney’s work at a rate of $520.00 per hour. (Opp., Fawaz Decl. ¶ 2.) The Court¿relies on its knowledge and
experience in¿determining¿the¿reasonable¿value of the legal services provided
under the circumstances in this case. (In re Marriage of Huntington (1992)
10 Cal.App.4th 1513, 1524 [“When the trial court is informed of the extent and
nature of the legal services rendered, it may rely on its own experience and
knowledge in determining their reasonable value.”].) The Court has discretion
to fix the amount of reasonable monetary sanctions.¿(Cornerstone Realty
Advisors, LLC v. Summit Heatlthcare Reit, Inc.¿(2020) 56
Cal.App.5th¿771, 791.)¿The Court finds a reasonable award¿is¿$2250.00, based
upon 5 hours of attorney’s work at a reasonable rate of $450.00 per
hour.   



V.        CONCLUSION



Light’s special motion to
strike is therefore DENIED.



State Farm’s request for
attorney’s fees and costs is GRANTED.  Light is ordered to pay State
Farm’s attorney’s fees in the amount of $2250.00 within 30 days.



State Farm is ordered to give notice.

Case Number: 25STCV29104    Hearing Date: June 24, 2026    Dept: 730

TENTATIVE 

 

  1. The Complaint 

 

On October 6, 2025, Plaintiff Collect Access LLC (“Plaintiff”) filed a Complaint against Defendant James Charles Lajevic a/k/a James Charles La Jevic a/k/a Jim A Lajavic a/k/a Jay Lajevic a/k/a James Talak d/b/a James C. Lajevic DMD (“Defendant Lajevic”) and DOES 1 through 10 (collectively, “Defendants”), alleging causes of action for: (1) Breach of Contract; (2) Money Due on Open Book Account; and (3) Money Due on an Account Stated. Specifically, the Complaint alleged that Defendant Lajevic entered into a Equipment Finance Agreement with Plaintiff’s Assignor Financial Pacific Leasing, Inc. on or about August 15, 2021, wherein he agreed to pay Financial Pacific Leasing, Inc. a sum of $66,795.36. (Compl., ¶¶9-11.) On or about February 29, 2024, Defendant Lajevic breached the agreement by failing to make payment as agreed, resulting in a due balance of $44,915.84. (Id., ¶12) or $39,993.14 (Id., ¶22 [listing the due balance as $39,993.14].) 

 

 

  1. Default Judgment 

 

All unnamed Doe defendants have been dismissed. 

 

In support of the default judgment package, Plaintiff submits the declaration of Moe Essa, its Legal Manager and Custodian of Records. Mr. Essa states that Plaintiff’s Assignor Financial Pacific Leasing Inc. entered into an Equipment Finance Agreement with Defendant Lajevic. (Essa Decl., ¶11, Ex. A.) Plaintiff also submitted the declaration of its counsel of record, Tappan Zee, Esq., attesting costs incurred, providing the interest calculation, and providing the attorney’s fee calculation in accordance with Local Rule 3.214. (Zee Decl., ¶¶2-8.) Nonetheless, Plaintiff fails to attach any agreement between Financial Pacific Leasing Inc. and Plaintiff demonstrating that the Equipment Finance Agreement was assigned to Plaintiff. Nor is there a declaration from Mr. Essa or another custodian of records for Plaintiff indicating a true and correct copy of such assignment agreement has been lost, misplaced, or damaged.  

 

 

  1. Conclusion 

 

Based on the foregoing, Plaintiff Collect Access LLC’s request for default judgment submitted on May 15, 2026 is DENIED without prejudice.
